Why AI strategy is a portfolio problem, not a roadmap

AI strategy that works looks like portfolio management under uncertainty: a small number of funded bets with provable metrics, a platform decision made before the third rebuild, and a governance model that lets teams move without an approval queue eating the quarter.

The deliverable is not a deck. It is a funded first slice with a signed baseline, an architecture direction your engineers respect, a gate model your risk team accepts, and a portfolio triage that killed the weak ideas on evidence rather than politics.
Below is the operating machinery of the portfolio: failure modes, the reference architecture for the decision system itself, and the console the steering committee reads.
Four ways AI portfolios stall at the board level
These are the governance and incentive failures, not the modeling ones — each countermeasure is a structural change to how the portfolio is funded and judged.

blocks.x: Standards the portfolio runs on — and where we deviate
The strategy layer standardizes decisions, not tools: gate definitions, evidence formats and re-baseline cadence. Where an enterprise standard already exists, it wins; the conditions are explicit.

blocks.caption: Enterprise AI Strategy & Roadmapping: default stack and the conditions under which we deviate
rows: Intake instrument
One-page provability canvas: metric, owner, data path, kill criterion
Two-hundred-line business cases — nobody reads them and they hide weak math
Risk tiering
Three tiers mapped to gates and evidence depth
Single committee for everything — the queue is the program's coffin
Platform call
Gateway-first with registry and eval spine before the third build
Waiting for 'the vendor landscape to settle' — it does not
Team topology
Platform team + 2–4 product-aligned slices
One central 'AI team' doing everything — it becomes the bottleneck
Board reporting
KPI ledger with spend, deltas and stop-loss record
Activity updates — they reward motion instead of value

blocks.x: How the strategy engagement runs

items: Weeks 1–2 — estate & portfolio audit
Existing models, spend, orphans; intake review; value hypothesis workshop
Weeks 3–4 — provability & risk model
Screen all candidates; risk tiers; kill list published with reasons
Weeks 5–6 — platform decision
Direction memo, residency map, vendor posture, migration path for pilots
Weeks 7–8 — first funded slice
Baseline signed, team staffed, gate dates set — delivery starts, not planning
Weeks 9–10 — operating model live
Gate reviews scheduled, stop-loss rules, board pack v1
Ongoing — quarterly rhythm
Portfolio review, platform reuse audit, capability re-plan
